You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: From $75 to $57, what signals has silver's latest pullback revealed?

TEXT:
Wednesday, July 1,
Spot Silver
is currently trading near $57.5/oz, with an intraday decline of about 1.9%, falling significantly from the early June highs; the daily chart also shows prices still close to the lower Bollinger band, MACD remains negative, and short-term pricing remains in a weak structure. Meanwhile, the 10-year US Treasury yield is around 4.47%, the
US Dollar Index
is around 101.30, and both interest rate and exchange rate variables continue to pressure the valuation of non-interest-bearing assets.
Silver pricing has switched to a growth-sensitive stage
The current core issue for silver is no longer just a linear game between inflation and interest rates, but whether "high financing costs can coexist with manufacturing resilience". This is also the fundamental reason why silver and gold trends tend to diverge. Gold primarily carries the attributes of credit, reserve, and safe haven, while silver is integrated into industrial chains including electronics, power, photovoltaic, automotive, and data centers, giving its price higher elasticity to growth expectations.
In May, the US manufacturing PMI recorded 54.0%, marking the fifth consecutive month of expansion, with the new orders index rising to 56.8%, the production index to 54.3%, and the price index still at a high level of 82.1%. In other words, the manufacturing side is not in total recession but in a complex combination of "demand persists, costs remain high, and employment is weak". For silver, this combination can both provide industrial demand support and amplify valuation pressure in a high interest rate environment.
Yields are still the ceiling for silver price rebounds
Silver has industrial attributes, but that does not mean it can escape interest rate pricing. In June, the Federal Reserve maintained the federal funds rate target range at 3.50% to 3.75% and emphasized that inflation remains above the 2% target, while stating that economic activity continues to expand at a solid pace. Such policy statements mean it is difficult for the market to quickly rebuild easing trades, and silver’s financial attributes continue to be restrained by real interest rates and the
US Dollar Index
.
Currently, the 10-year US Treasury yield is around 4.47%, and the two-year yield remains above 4%, so the pressure of the yield curve on precious metals has not disappeared.
US Dollar Index
remaining above 101 also dampens the willingness of non-dollar funds to chase silver prices. The drop in silver price from above $75 in early June to around $57 is essentially the result of a simultaneous squeeze from previously high valuations, long positions, and interest rate revaluation. A short-term low price does not automatically mean that pressure has been fully released—the key lies in whether manufacturing data can prove industrial demand is sufficient to offset tighter financial conditions.
The key point of ISM data is not strength or weakness, but whether it worsens
The market’s focus on the US ISM manufacturing data tonight is not because a single month’s reading can determine the direction of silver, but because it will affect traders’ repricing of silver’s industrial attribute. If the data only falls moderately from 54.0 to near market expectations, it more likely signifies a slowdown in expansion momentum rather than a breakdown in demand. For silver, a slowdown in expansion and the end of expansion are two completely different pricing scenarios.
What’s more important is the sub-index structure. If new orders continue to expand, it means corporate capital expenditure and downstream restocking still have a basis; if the production index remains above 50, it indicates industrial end-demand is not obviously stalling; and if the price index continues to run high, it limits room for policy shifts, keeping silver prices capped by interest rates. Currently, silver is not simply a bet on growth or a bet on rate cuts, but is searching for a new equilibrium point between "industrial demand resilience" and "high interest rate suppression".
Structural demand remains, but the photovoltaic narrative has been repriced
From a medium- to long-term perspective, silver is still embedded in the industrial narrative. Industry institutions estimate that global silver demand in 2026 will be roughly flat, with industrial processing demand possibly declining by 2% to around 650 million ounces, mainly due to silver-saving and substitution effects from the photovoltaic sector; but data centers, artificial intelligence technologies, automotive, and other electrification applications will continue to support some industrial end uses.
This means the structural logic of silver has not disappeared; it has shifted from single photovoltaic-driven demand to diversified industrial scenario support. On the trading side, it is even more important to distinguish "long-term usage expansion" from "short-term price pressure". If financing costs stay high, the long-term story of industrial demand is unlikely to immediately translate into a price trend; but if manufacturing maintains moderate expansion, silver may continue to retain higher cyclical elasticity than gold.
Editor: Zhu Henan
